questions.stem: Which item is one of the six rights of medication administration?
questions.why: Patient, drug, dose, route, time, and documentation. Documentation is the one people forget, and it is the one that exists after the call is over.

options.why: Diagnosis is not one of the six; the right drug is.
The list concerns the patient and the drug, not the disposition.
Packaging is not one of the six rights.

questions.stem: What separates an antiseptic from a disinfectant?
questions.why: Antiseptics go on skin before an invasive procedure. Disinfectants clean equipment and surfaces and would damage living tissue.

options.t: Antiseptics clean equipment while disinfectants prep the patient's skin
options.why: That reverses the two.

options.t: They are interchangeable names for the same class of agent
options.why: They are distinguished precisely because they are not interchangeable.

options.t: Antiseptics kill spores while disinfectants leave spores intact
options.why: Spore-killing is not the distinction taught here.

options.t: Antiseptics go on the patient; disinfectants do not

questions.stem: How much crystalloid replaces a given volume of blood loss?
questions.why: Three to one, because roughly two thirds of an isotonic crystalloid moves out of the vascular space. Blood replaces blood one for one; crystalloid does not.

options.why: That would leave the patient more depleted than when you started.
Crystalloid leaves the vascular space, so equal replacement falls short.
The taught ratio is higher than two to one.

questions.stem: What is the stated goal of a fluid bolus in this program?
questions.why: Boluses maintain perfusion — mentation, pulses, urine output. They are not given to make the blood pressure read normal, which is a different and more dangerous goal.

options.why: Dilution is not the purpose of a resuscitation bolus.

options.t: To replace the entire volume lost before transport
options.why: Full replacement is not achievable or intended in the field.

options.t: To raise the blood pressure to a normal number
options.why: Chasing a number can push clots off and dilute clotting factors.

questions.stem: Which fluids does the lecture list as isotonic?
questions.why: Those three are the isotonic solutions named. D5W is isotonic in the bag; the dextrose is metabolized quickly once infused, which is why its behavior in the body differs from the label.

options.t: Normal saline, lactated Ringer's, and D5NS
options.why: D5NS is hypertonic once in the bag.
3 percent saline is hypertonic.

options.t: Normal saline, lactated Ringer's, and D5W

options.why: Half normal saline is hypotonic.

questions.stem: What are the drop factors for microdrip and macrodrip tubing?
questions.why: Microdrip is 60 drops per mL — the small drops, for controlled rates and pediatric patients. Macrodrip is 10 or 15 — the big drops, for volume.

options.why: That reverses the two.

options.t: Micro 15; macro 60, with no other sizes made
options.why: Microdrip is the 60 drop set.
Macrodrip sets are 10 or 15 in this program.

questions.stem: At what angle does the catheter enter, and what happens after flashback?
questions.why: Enter at 45 to get through the skin, then flatten to 15 to follow the vein rather than punching out the far side. Advance the catheter, not the needle.

options.why: Raising the angle after entry pushes the needle through the back wall.
A perpendicular entry is intraosseous technique, not venous.
The angle changes after flashback rather than staying fixed.

questions.stem: How much fluid does a saline lock hold?
questions.why: Roughly 2 mL. That is the volume that has to be pushed through before a drug given into the lock actually reaches the patient.

options.why: That is less than the lock's actual dead space.
20 mL is the adenosine flush volume.
10 mL is a flush volume, not the lock's capacity.

questions.stem: How is the patient positioned for external jugular cannulation, and where is the puncture made?
questions.why: Head-down distends the vein and reduces air embolism risk. Puncture midway between the angle of the jaw and the midclavicular line, with the vein tamponaded above the clavicle to make it stand out.

options.t: Sitting fully upright, midway between the jaw angle and the midclavicular line
options.why: Sitting up collapses the vein and raises the risk of an air embolism.

options.t: Supine with the head raised, just below the angle of the jaw
options.why: Head-up empties the vein rather than distending it.

options.t: Supine head-down, puncturing directly over the clavicle itself
options.why: That is too low and sits over structures you do not want to hit.

options.t: Head-down, midway between jaw angle and midclavicular line

questions.stem: A patient develops fever and chills within 30 minutes of an infusion starting. What has happened?
questions.why: Pyrogens — contaminants in the fluid or the set — produce fever and chills within about thirty minutes of starting. Stop the infusion, keep the line with new fluid and tubing, and save the bag.

options.why: Overload presents with dyspnea and crackles rather than fever and chills.

options.t: An allergic reaction to the catheter material
options.why: A latex or material reaction presents with local or systemic allergy signs, not this timing and fever.
An air embolism presents suddenly with respiratory distress and hypotension.

questions.stem: You puncture an artery instead of a vein. How long must direct pressure be held?
questions.why: Withdraw the catheter and hold direct pressure for five minutes or more. Arterial pressure will reopen a site that has not fully sealed.

options.why: Longer than the standard taught here.
One minute is not long enough for an arterial puncture to seal.
Thirty seconds is a venous site, not an arterial one.

questions.stem: A patient becomes dyspneic with crackles during an infusion. What are the three management steps?
questions.why: Circulatory overload: slow the infusion, sit the patient up so gravity keeps fluid out of the upper lungs, and oxygenate. Reassess lung sounds after each change.

options.t: Slow the rate, raise the head, give high-flow oxygen
Slow the rate, lay the patient flat, give a fluid challenge
options.why: More fluid is the opposite of what circulatory overload needs.

options.t: Raise the head, increase the rate, give high-flow oxygen
options.why: Increasing the rate adds to the volume already overwhelming the patient.

options.t: Stop the line entirely, lay the patient flat, give high-flow oxygen
options.why: Laying the patient flat worsens the pulmonary congestion.

questions.stem: Which catheter sizes does the lecture list for pediatric patients?
questions.why: 20 through 26 gauge. Smaller catheters take smaller veins but deliver volume more slowly, which is the tradeoff to state out loud when volume is what the child needs.

options.why: Those are general adult sizes.
Those are adult trauma sizes.
18 is larger than the pediatric range given.
